title: Selective Language Damage with Parameter-Decomposition Subcomponents
text: Short summary · PDF · Study guide

title: Selective Language Damage with Parameter-Decomposition Subcomponents
text:
1 Introduction
Removing parameters important for Spanish raises perplexity in Portuguese and Italian (Zhang et al. 2024, Table 11). This spillover matters for model editing, where a goal is to preserve predictions outside the intended scope of a change (Yao et al. 2023, sec. 2). An edit that does little to Spanish might also spare Portuguese. Matching the edits on Spanish loss makes their effects on Portuguese easier to interpret.
adVersarial Parameter Decomposition (VPD) approximates weight matrices with sums of rank-one subcomponents. It rewards approximations that can use few subcomponents on a given input (Bushnaq et al. 2026, sec. 2).1 Bushnaq used a subcomponent’s interpretation label to select a direction that suppressed German with little change in English, French or Spanish, though Italian prediction also worsened (Bushnaq 2026). The selector tested here ranks directions numerically using only target and English text. For German, Spanish and French targets, the corresponding tests of collateral damage use Dutch, Portuguese and Italian. Figures and tables call this second language in each pair protected.

title: Selective Language Damage with Parameter-Decomposition Subcomponents
text:
2 Methods

2.1 Model and data
Goodfire’s base model is a four-layer, 67M-parameter decoder-only language model trained on a subset of the Pile. Its VPD dictionary contains 38,912 subcomponents across 24 weight matrices (Bushnaq et al. 2026, sec. 3.1; Gao et al. 2020). Damage is the rise from the base model in mean next-token cross-entropy (CE), in nat/token.
Each European Parliament session date contributes one window per language, with 256 next-token predictions. Windows begin at the same aligned speaker turn, then each language is tokenized and truncated independently (Koehn 2005). For each target, selection and training use three overlapping draws of 64 out of 128 training windows. All draws share 256 English windows from Europarl, WikiText-2 and the Pile (Merity et al. 2017; Gao et al. 2020). The learned updates use a different seed for each draw.


2.2 Selecting a subcomponent
A rank-one subcomponent \(A_c=u_cv_c^\top\) reads one scalar \(v_c^\top x\) from the input and adds \(u_c(v_c^\top x)\) to the output. In its weight matrix \(W\), the original coefficient is 1. An edit \(W'=W+\alpha A_c\) changes the coefficient to \(1+\alpha\), keeping both directions fixed. A zero coefficient removes the contribution and a negative coefficient reverses it.
A candidate ranks highly when a small coefficient change is expected to raise target loss at little cost in English predictions. If \(g_c\) is the derivative of mean target CE along \(A_c\), an edit of size \(\alpha\) changes target CE by approximately \(\alpha g_c\). On English text, the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence from the base model is approximately \(q_c\alpha^2/2\), where \(q_c\) estimates directional Fisher curvature. The score is \[\frac{g_c^2}{q_c+\varepsilon\lVert A_c\rVert_F^2}.\] The floor in the denominator limits the influence of small curvature estimates. After re-ranking the top 64 candidates on further English text, the search tests them in order on target training text at \(\alpha=\operatorname{sign}(g_c)\,a\), increasing \(a\) up to 2. The first direction to reach 1 nat/token of damage is selected, or the first to reach 0.5 if none reaches 1.


2.3 Comparison methods
Rank-one LoRA (Hu et al. 2022) learns both factors of an update in layer 0’s attention output matrix, matching the rank and location of all three selected VPD subcomponents. Full-matrix fine-tuning can change all 24 matrices. Both train for 200 steps with a hinge penalty for target CE rises below 1 nat/token on each window and an equally weighted penalty on English KL divergence. The neuron comparator ranks MLP neurons by the difference in activation frequency between target text and English, then reduces the output weights of the top-ranked neurons (Tang et al. 2024; Kojima et al. 2024). A fourth comparator applies the VPD selection rule after random signed permutations of the input and output coordinates within each dictionary matrix. This preserves the subcomponents’ norms and pairwise angles while changing their alignment with the model’s weights.


2.4 Calibration and evaluation
Each edit must raise mean CE on 32 target validation windows to within 0.02 nat/token of \(\tau=0.5\) or 1. The edit then stays fixed. For each target, all three draws selected the same subcomponent and the same two doses, yielding six distinct VPD edits. Three reduced the coefficient while keeping it positive, and three reversed its sign (Table 2).

Earlier work used Dutch, Portuguese and Italian development text, as well as Dutch and Italian text from NTREX (Federmann et al. 2022). I had previously selected the German subcomponent with Dutch in view. On 11 October 2026, I fixed the methods and main analysis before the 64-date development evaluation. The same edits were evaluated once on 58 further dates under an amendment fixed before parsing those windows. My records document this chronology without an independently timestamped preregistration.


An edit was eligible for confirmation only if mean English CE rose by at most 0.1 nat/token on every development and confirmation check. Each contrast is the difference in related-language CE rise (VPD minus comparator) for a given pair and dose, averaged over matched, eligible draws and then over dates. Simultaneous 95% intervals resample session dates with the edits, training runs and language pairs held fixed. The prespecified tolerance for each edit’s achieved target effect on evaluation text was \(\tau\pm0.1\) nat/token.

text:
3 Results

3.1 Related-language damage
On the 58 new dates, all matched edits in the main comparison passed the English checks and met the target tolerance (Figure 1). The six VPD edits raised related-language CE by 0.0003–0.0053 nat/token. The individual comparator edits raised it by 0.027–0.236 for LoRA, 0.058–0.407 for full-matrix fine-tuning and 0.423–0.876 for neuron edits.






Figure 1: Cross-entropy increases on 58 confirmation dates (vertical axis logarithmic). For each language pair and calibration target \(\tau\), three draws yield one shared VPD edit and three comparator edits per method.




All 18 estimated contrasts had simultaneous 95% intervals below zero. At \(\tau=1\), for example, the German VPD edit raised Dutch CE by 0.089 nat/token less than LoRA (VPD minus LoRA, −0.100 to −0.077). Each fixed VPD edit enters three contrasts. The six planned randomized-dictionary contrasts have no estimates. None of the nine randomized searches reached even 0.5 nat/token within the dose limit.



3.2 Achieved target effects
Meeting the per-edit tolerance still allows two methods to differ in achieved target damage. In a post hoc analysis, 15 of 18 simultaneous intervals for the difference in achieved target CE rise lay wholly within ±0.1 nat/token. In all three exceptions the mean target CE rise was larger for VPD (Figure 2). Each VPD edit raised target CE on every confirmation window. Related-language CE rose on 30–47 of the 58 windows per edit, with a maximum single-window rise of 0.037 nat/token.






Figure 2: Whiskers give simultaneous 95% intervals over session dates. In the top row, negative values mean less related-language damage from VPD, and scales vary by comparator. The shaded band tests post hoc agreement in target damage.





3.3 Preservation of English predictions
CE measures loss on the observed next token. KL divergence \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\mathrm{base}}\,\|\,p_{\mathrm{edit}})\) measures the change across the full prediction distribution. In this post hoc comparison, LoRA and full-matrix fine-tuning each preserved English predictions better than VPD in all 18 target–dose–draw comparisons on the new dates. Both objectives directly penalized English KL. The VPD edits’ mean English KL was below 0.001 nat/token (Table 1). On the related languages, all 18 simultaneous intervals for VPD minus comparator KL lay below zero.

3.4 Stronger learned comparators
The original runs chose the highest learning rate tested for LoRA and the lowest for full-matrix fine-tuning. An exploratory comparison on the previously evaluated development dates used 2,000 training steps, wider learning-rate grids, a larger hinge margin and three seeds per draw. This recipe reduced mean related-language damage in five of six target–dose combinations for LoRA and all six for full-matrix fine-tuning. VPD still caused less damage in all 12 comparisons, with mean target effects differing by at most 0.07 nat/token. Several settings changed together and convergence remains unestablished.

title: Selective Language Damage with Parameter-Decomposition Subcomponents
text:
4 Discussion

4.1 What the choice of direction contributes
Within the VPD dictionary, selecting the subcomponent most aligned with a learned update or selecting by the target-minus-English difference in VPD’s learned causal-importance scores caused at least as much related-language damage wherever comparisons were possible. At similar target effects, the importance rule raised related-language CE by 0.48–1.37 nat/token more than the main selector on the new dates. These comparisons are descriptive and some include fewer than three draws.
Bushnaq’s previously reported direction in layer 3 (attention value, index 513) caused less Dutch damage than the selected direction in layer 0 (attention output, index 268). At a German validation target of 0.5 nat/token, a post hoc scan found Dutch CE rises of 0.0012 and 0.0036 nat/token, respectively, on the 64 development dates. The scan left achieved German test damage, English eligibility and Italian damage unmeasured.

Two further controls tested directions outside the VPD dictionary on development text. A rank-one direction computed from target gradients and approximate English Fisher curvature (Martens and Grosse 2015) damaged the related languages more, but borrowed the selected VPD subcomponent’s norm and the selector’s curvature floor. Every edit to a singular component of the weight matrices that reached the target effect exceeded the English CE limit. These controls leave the decomposition’s contribution open.



4.2 Scope

Six fixed subcomponent edits spared related-language predictions better than the tested comparators at similar mean target damage. The learned updates better preserved the English predictions their objectives protected. Providing those objectives with related-language examples could change this ordering. Confirmation tests these edits on new parliamentary text in one model. How the selector performs on new languages or models, and whether the directions implement a language-specific mechanism, remain open.


Code and data. Per-date measurements support a replay of the analysis, including the post hoc window and German shortlist checks. Rerunning the confirmatory model evaluation requires the unpublished text windows. Study guide

AI assistance. I used OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude for planning, coding, analysis and writing, and Scientific Agent Skills (Kassis et al. 2026) for manuscript review.

title: Selective Language Damage with Parameter-Decomposition Subcomponents
text:
Appendix — Estimation and comparison details
Selection and tuning. The Fisher estimate averages squared directional scores from eight model-sampled label sets per English window (Martens 2020; Kunstner et al. 2019). The floor \(\varepsilon\) is the first percentile of \(q_c/\lVert A_c\rVert_F^2\). Shortlisted candidates are ranked again using the larger of two curvature estimates, the second from 256 other English windows. GPU-dependent label sampling affects reproducibility. Selector reruns verified the first German draw on the L40S for VPD and one randomized dictionary. The curvature check failed on the tested A10 and L4.
For neuron edits, calibration chooses the smallest power-of-two count from 1 to 256 whose full removal reaches \(\tau\), then scales the output weights. For each target, the learning rate with the lowest English validation KL at \(\tau=1\) on draw 0 was 0.003 for LoRA and \(10^{-6}\) for full-matrix fine-tuning. Calibration can scale the learned update down.

Evaluation. The development English CE checks use 64 Europarl windows, 32 WikiText-2 windows and 512 Pile documents. Confirmation uses English from the 58 further dates (48 main and 10 reserve, analyzed together). The Pile contains European Parliament text, so pretraining overlap is possible (Gao et al. 2020, sec. 2.17). The main analysis specified four comparators, three language pairs and two doses. Intervals use 2,000 shared date bootstrap resamples with a max-\(|t|\) critical value (Efron 1979; Montiel Olea and Plagborg-Møller 2019, supplement, Algorithm 3). The post hoc family uses 20,000 resamples per dataset. Its simultaneous intervals cover 18 method–pair–dose comparisons across three outcomes jointly: achieved target CE, related-language CE and related-language KL.


Alternative directions and training. The alignment rules normalize each dictionary subcomponent and select the one with the largest absolute inner product with a learned update. One rule uses a full-matrix update and the other uses a LoRA update across all 24 matrices. The importance rule adapts Bushnaq’s top-16 ranking to one subcomponent. These comparisons use eligible, matched draws with a separate simultaneous correction. The expanded training comparison uses unpaired means over matched, usable runs. Excluding seven of 27 LoRA runs whose final English validation KL exceeded twice its minimum from step 100 onward gave the same direction of effect. I specified the exploratory comparisons before the runs and fixed their analysis before development readout, with selection outcomes and validation effects already known.

title: Transferring Learned Repairs Between Fine-Tunes
text: Short summary · PDF · Study guide

title: Transferring Learned Repairs Between Fine-Tunes
text:
1 Introduction
A repair is an extra weight update that restores a capability damaged by fine-tuning while preserving the intended change. If the same recipe causes similar damage on a second run, an earlier repair could save work in two ways. Its directions might already be right, so that only their strengths need fitting. Or the directions might give training a head start, even if they eventually need to change. Fitting a new repair from scratch tests how much that head start is worth.
Scaled weight updates have been used in task arithmetic (Ilharco et al. 2023) and safety repair (Bhardwaj et al. 2024; Wang et al. 2026). Transferring a fitted initialization has a precedent in soft prompts (Vu et al. 2022). Here the same learned donor repair supplies both comparisons, and the outcome is recovery of next-token prediction loss.

title: Transferring Learned Repairs Between Fine-Tunes
text:
2 Experimental design
Three independent fine-tunes began from Goodfire’s four-layer, 67M-parameter language model (Bushnaq et al. 2026, sec. 3.1). They used the same objective and selected learning rate, with different seeds and samples of Europarl debates (Koehn 2005). Each deliberately raised German cross-entropy (CE, the mean next-token prediction loss). Dutch was outside the objective, so an increase in Dutch CE measures collateral damage. One fine-tune, the donor, supplied a repair learned on 73,728 prediction positions. The other two were targets for transfer.
The repair adds one learned update to each of 24 attention and MLP weight matrices. Each update has the LoRA form \(E_m=b_m a_m^\top\) with rank at most one (Hu et al. 2022). Applied to an input \(x\), the repair reads one scalar \(a_m^\top x\) and adds \(b_m(a_m^\top x)\) to the output. A coefficient can strengthen, weaken or reverse this change. Training the vectors can also change which inputs produce a response and where the response goes.
Every target repair had to fit within the Frobenius norm of the target’s fine-tuning update, computed across all 24 matrices. Methods that reused the donor started from the same repair, scaled down uniformly if needed to satisfy that cap. Scalar fitting learned one coefficient per matrix (24 parameters). Donor initialization trained both vectors (55,296 parameters). Fresh fitting trained both vectors from a zero update, with random input vectors and zero output vectors. One control trained only the donor’s output vectors. Another trained both vectors from random directions matched to the donor vectors’ lengths.
Fitting minimized three equally weighted KL divergences between next-token distributions. The teacher was the base model for Dutch, and the fine-tuned model for German and a pool of four languages the fine-tune sought to preserve (English, French, Spanish and Italian). Dutch CE recovery measures the fraction of the fine-tune’s excess Dutch loss that the repair removed. A repair with 0% recovery leaves all the extra loss in place. At 100% recovery, Dutch CE returns to the base-model value.
The targets had disjoint fine-tuning dates. They shared the repair-fitting windows, the checkpoint-selection windows and the final evaluation windows. Repair fitting used nested sets of 256, 512 or 2,048 prediction positions. At each step cap (50, 100, 200 or 600), checkpoints from four learning-rate runs were eligible for selection. Checkpoint selection used 32 separate Europarl session dates to rank candidates by Dutch CE recovery subject to limits on German and retain-language changes. The final evaluation measured recovery and rechecked those limits on 92 further dates. Paired 95% bootstrap intervals resample those dates jointly across repairs within each target. They describe uncertainty over evaluation text for the fitted repairs.

title: Transferring Learned Repairs Between Fine-Tunes
text:
3 Results

3.1 How much can fixed directions recover?
The two fine-tunes raised Dutch CE by 0.187 and 0.189 nat/token. Applying the donor repair without further fitting removed 86.3% of this damage on the first target and 58.6% on the second. The primary test compared donor initialization with an expanded scalar search at the full budget of 2,048 fit tokens and a 600-step cap for ordinary training. The scalar search included 48 ordinary checkpoints and two further projected-gradient runs, giving it the larger search budget. Both extra runs met their stopping criteria on each target, and both selected repairs on each target passed the evaluation constraints.



Table 1: Excess Dutch loss recovered at 2,048 fit tokens and a 600-step cap for ordinary runs. Scalar fitting included two extra candidates. The difference is donor minus scalar. Brackets give 95% bootstrap intervals over dates within each target.

Both paired intervals lie entirely above the prespecified margin of 3 percentage points (pp) (Table 1). The extra scalar search kept the ordinary checkpoint on the first target and raised recovery from 77.3% to 78.4% on the second. The gap was already visible on the fitting text. There the selected scalar repairs removed 87.0% and 79.2% of Dutch KL divergence from the base model, while every method that trained a vector removed at least 98.4%. Other coefficient choices or a larger norm cap could give different results.
Across the three token budgets, with a 600-step cap, ordinary scalar fitting stayed below 90% recovery on both targets, while donor initialization and fresh fitting exceeded 95% (Figure 2).
Training only the donor’s output vectors recovered 97.1% and 97.4% at full budget. Most of the improvement over rescaling was therefore attainable while the input directions stayed fixed.


3.2 When does the donor start help?
At 256 fit tokens and 50 steps, donor initialization recovered 4.4 and 4.1 pp more than fresh fitting on the two targets. It also led the norm-matched random start by 4.9 and 4.5 pp. At this setting there was one seed per control and one shared set of fitting positions.






Figure 1: Differences in the share of excess Dutch loss recovered, in percentage points. Fresh and random starts use their first seed. Whiskers give paired 95% bootstrap intervals over 92 evaluation dates.



With 2,048 tokens and up to 600 steps, the first fresh start recovered 97.2% and 97.4%. The donor’s paired leads were 1.1 pp [0.8, 1.3] and 1.4 pp [1.1, 1.7]. Both intervals fit inside the prespecified ±2 pp equivalence band. A second fresh seed recovered 98.2% and 98.0%. Against the first norm-matched random start at full budget, the donor led by 0.6 pp [0.3, 0.9] on the primary target and 0.01 pp [−0.26, 0.28] on replication. The first fresh seed reused the random input vectors from which the donor had originally been trained, so its comparison with the donor measures the value of the whole fitted start.


3.3 What does reuse save?
The first fresh fit at full budget served as the quality reference. A setting qualified if its selected repair passed the evaluation constraints and the lower bound of its paired recovery difference from the reference exceeded −2 pp. After evaluation I chose the cheapest qualifying setting separately for each method and cost measure.
On each target, the fewest fit-token presentations needed by donor initialization were 51,200 (256 positions × 50 steps × four learning rates). Fresh fitting needed 409,600 (2,048 × 50 × four). Allowing 600 steps let both methods qualify with just 256 distinct fitting positions. On this grid, donor initialization needed one eighth as many presentations as fresh fitting to reach the reference. The minimum amount of distinct text was the same.
Training the donor repair had itself cost 3,686,400 presentations. If each new target saved the observed 358,400 presentations and the donor fine-tune already existed, reuse would pay back this cost on the eleventh target. Changing the reference to the second fresh seed in a post hoc analysis moved payback to the fifth target. The experiment did not measure an end-to-end time saving. Cost accounting

title: Transferring Learned Repairs Between Fine-Tunes
text:
4 Discussion
The output-only fits inherited the donor’s input directions and its trained output vectors. How much did the input directions themselves contribute? Two output-only fits starting from zero outputs, one with donor inputs and one with norm-matched random inputs, would test that question from identical initial updates.
Bushnaq scaled a German-related component from a decomposition of this same model’s base weights (Bushnaq et al. 2026; Bushnaq 2026). Here the directions came from fitting a repair to Dutch text. A corresponding test for a decomposition-derived component would compare its attainable training loss with that of a trainable update under a common rank and norm budget.
The evidence comes from one donor that had already passed a recovery check, two independently trained targets, one recipe and one base model. Additional donors, training windows and seeds would be needed to estimate how often the early advantage recurs. The measured outcome is prediction loss on these languages. The experiment leaves the internal mechanism of repair and transfer to other capabilities open.
AI assistance. I used OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude for planning, coding, analysis and writing, and Scientific Agent Skills (Kassis et al. 2026) for manuscript review.

title: Transferring Learned Repairs Between Fine-Tunes
text:
Appendix — Selection, checks and reproduction
The study guide links the recipe, token windows, donor repair and saved measurements, with commands for replay and retraining.

Checkpoint selection
The fine-tunes trained full-matrix updates for 200 steps, penalizing a German CE increase below 1 nat/token and drift from the base model on the four retain languages. The donor repair passed an 80% Dutch CE recovery threshold on 112 dates. The target fine-tunes used disjoint sets of 64 dates each drawn from the pool originally set aside for donor evaluation. Target repair fitting, selection and final evaluation used dates outside the donor sets.
Half the target repair’s fit tokens came from Dutch and a quarter each from German and the pooled retain languages. Full-batch Adam (Kingma and Ba 2015) supplied checkpoints every 50 steps. On selection text a candidate had to preserve 90–110% of the German CE increase and reduce Dutch KL from the base. Its German KL from the fine-tune, \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\text{fine-tuned}}\|p_{\text{repair}})\), had to be at most 5% of the corresponding KL with the base model in place of the repair. Qualifying checkpoints were ranked by Dutch CE recovery, with ties broken by smaller norm and then listing order. The first of the top five with a CE increase of at most 0.01 nat/token above the fine-tuned model on every retain language advanced to evaluation.


Primary comparison and uncertainty
For the primary comparison to count, the lower 95% bound on the target’s Dutch CE increase had to reach 0.025 nat/token. It reached 0.178 and 0.180 on the two targets. The selected repairs had to pass the selection constraints again on evaluation text. Each of the two additional scalar runs, starting from the donor coefficients and the best ordinary checkpoint by fit loss, had to satisfy the prespecified numerical checks. The runs stopped on relative loss decrease in three cases and at the line-search floor with sufficiently small projected gradient in the fourth. These local checks apply within the tested norm cap. Evaluation constraints and results · Optimizer settings · Optimizer results
Each of 5,000 bootstrap replicates computed recovery from mean losses over resampled dates (Efron 1979). Five specified secondary comparisons had a ±2 pp equivalence margin. The protocol set this margin and the 3 pp primary margin without a separate empirical justification. Secondary intervals are descriptive and unadjusted for multiple comparisons. My dated records place these rules before target fine-tuning and evaluation. They lack independent timestamps. Secondary contrasts


Cost accounting
The minimum of 256 distinct fit positions for fresh fitting depended on the reference. Its lower bounds cleared the −2 pp cutoff by just 0.015 and 0.043 pp. Using the second fresh seed as the reference raised the minimum to 2,048 for fresh fitting while donor initialization still qualified at 256. Unique-token costs also include 57,344 shared selection positions. Presentations count training across the four learning rates and exclude selection forward passes. Estimated GPU seconds include training and selection but exclude final target evaluation, the initial damage check and exploration of other settings. On the two targets, estimated times at the cheapest qualifying settings were 14.5 and 13.9 seconds from the donor, versus 16.8 and 17.1 from scratch. The estimated one-time donor cost was 336 GPU seconds. Complete cost comparison · Recovery against training cost


Portuguese (post hoc)
Portuguese took no part in fitting or checkpoint selection. On the same 92 evaluation dates, the full-budget scalar repairs raised Portuguese CE over the respective fine-tunes by 0.00115 and 0.00114 nat/token. Donor initialization lowered it by 0.00064 and 0.00069, and the first fresh fits lowered it by 0.00135 and 0.00142. The six pointwise 95% intervals exclude zero. title: Some Studies of Language Model Weight Edits
text:
Some Studies of Language Model Weight Edits
  I tested how weight edits affect predictions across languages and whether a correction learned for one fine-tune can help another.
  First published 14 October 2026 · Updated 18 November 2026



  
    Selective language editing
    Worsening a model’s German predictions also affected its Dutch. How much depended on the edit. Across three language pairs, changing one weight subcomponent did the least damage to the related language when the edits were calibrated to the same target loss increase on validation text. LoRA and full-matrix fine-tuning preserved English predictions better.

    Repair transfer

Training the repair vectors recovered more than rescaling them along their original directions. With little data and few steps, the earlier repair gave training a head start.     About these studies
    The work presented here is my attempt to understand interpretability and model editing methods more deeply. By building on recent advances and trying to find something new, I also learn what others have done before me. For me, the best way to learn is through practice.
    Although these studies are written in the form of research papers, I’m not yet confident that I can call them rigorous scientific work. I’m sharing them in the hope that they may be useful to someone besides me.
  
  
    AI assistance
    I made extensive use of Codex with GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, as well as Claude Code with Opus 5.5, throughout this work. I personally supervised the experiments and guided their direction based on the results and the questions I wanted to explore.
    Most of the text was also written with AI assistance and went through several rounds of careful editing. I hope attentive readers will forgive me for that.

section: Three ways to fit a repair
text:
Three ways to fit a repair
The two targets reuse a repair learned on one earlier fine-tune, the donor. All three fine-tunes used the same base model and recipe, with different seeds and samples of Europarl text.
The repair adds a rank-one update \(E=ba^\top\) to each of 24 weight matrices. The input vector \(a\) reads one scalar \(a^\top x\) from \(x\). The output vector \(b\) writes the correction \(Ex=b(a^\top x)\).

Scalar-only fitting learns one multiplier per matrix to rescale or reverse the donor’s correction along the same line.
Donor initialization refits both vectors from their donor values. Their lengths and directions can change.
Fresh initialization also fits both vectors. It starts with a random input vector and a zero output vector in each matrix.

title: Selective language editing
text:
Edit one rank-one subcomponent
Goodfire’s adVersarial Parameter Decomposition (VPD) expresses a weight matrix \(W\) as a sum of rank-one subcomponents and a residual. The training objective favors using few subcomponents to approximate the computation for each input.
A subcomponent \(A=u_{\mathrm{out}}v_{\mathrm{in}}^\top\) reads one number from the input \(x\) with \(v_{\mathrm{in}}^\top x\). That number scales the output vector \(u_{\mathrm{out}}\).
\[
Ax = u_{\mathrm{out}}\bigl(v_{\mathrm{in}}^\top x\bigr).
\]
The edit scales \(A\) by a single coefficient \(c\), changing many weights at once.
\[
W_{\mathrm{edited}} = (W-A) + cA.
\]
At \(c=1\) the matrix is unchanged, at \(c=0\) the contribution is removed, and at \(c<0\) its sign reverses.

title: Selective language editing
section: Compare edits at similar target damage
text:
Compare edits at similar target damage
The selector ranks subcomponents by how much a small coefficient change is predicted to raise target loss for a given change in English predictions. It tests leading candidates on target training text. The comparison included three other ways to worsen target predictions while preserving English.

Rank-one LoRA learns a new pair of input and output vectors for the same matrix as the VPD edit.
Full-matrix fine-tuning can change every entry in the 24 attention and feed-forward weight matrices.
Neuron edits reduce output weights for neurons that activate more often on target text than on English.

An edit could spare Dutch by barely affecting German. Calibration sets the strength of each edit to raise mean next-token prediction loss (cross-entropy) by 0.5 or 1 nat/token on target-language validation text.
The final comparison used the fixed edits on text from 58 held-out European Parliament session dates. The related languages were absent from selection and training for these runs. In earlier work I used development text from those languages and took Dutch performance into account when choosing the German subcomponent. Data and prior access
